body: {"total":8,"records":[{"title":"Structured versus usual validation of syndromic surveillance alerts: a randomised comparison in a regional public health unit","authors":"Lindqvist-Achebe M, Osei-Carvalho R, Brandt-Nakamura E","year":2020,"venue":"Brackenmoor Surveillance Practice Journal","doi":"10.5555/jphsp.2020.0217","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"Over 20 weeks, 412 syndromic surveillance alerts in one regional public health unit were randomised individually to a structured validation protocol or to usual review by the epidemiologist on duty. Randomising alerts to a structured protocol shortened the median time to a validation decision from 96 to 42 minutes. Escalations were similar (6 against 7 per 100 alerts). Two true events were dismissed at the first alert in the protocol arm and three in the usual arm, too few to compare. Epidemiologists reported applying parts of the protocol to usual-review alerts after the first month, which may have reduced the difference."},{"title":"Positive predictive value of syndromic surveillance alerts for confirmed outbreaks: a five-year review","authors":"Kowalczyk-Obi T, Fairbanks-Mensah L","year":2017,"venue":"Epidemiology and Surveillance Notes","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We linked 8,900 alerts from a syndromic surveillance system over five years to outbreak reports from laboratories and local health units. Four percent of alerts corresponded to a confirmed outbreak or cluster within 14 days. Most false alerts arose from reporting artefacts, duplicate records and changes in emergency department coding. Gastrointestinal alerts in people aged 65 and over had the highest predictive value, often linked to care homes. The authors suggest that validation should concentrate on excluding artefacts quickly and on alerts in settings with vulnerable populations."},{"title":"Validation practices for syndromic surveillance signals: a survey of 62 public health agencies","authors":"Haddad-Lindgren S, Mwale-Oduya P, Ferreira-Hart K","year":2022,"venue":"Wrenmouth Public Health Informatics Reports","doi":"10.5555/phir.2022.0063","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We surveyed 62 public health agencies about how syndromic surveillance alerts are validated. Seventy-one percent had no written validation procedure. The median reported time per alert was 45 minutes, with a range from under 10 minutes to more than three hours, and agencies rarely measured how often real events were dismissed. Agencies with a written procedure reported more consistent escalation decisions but not shorter times. Respondents identified duplicate records and coding changes as the commonest causes of false alerts and staff shortages at weekends as the commonest cause of delay."},{"title":"Panel review as a reference standard for outbreak signals: agreement and hindsight bias","authors":"Sandoval-Pike R, Adeyemi-Holm J","year":2019,"venue":"Tamsford Epidemiologic Methods Letters","doi":"10.5555/eml.2019.0145","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We asked panels of three epidemiologists to classify 300 past syndromic alerts as true or false signals, first without and then with knowledge of later outbreak reports. Agreement between panels without outcome knowledge was moderate (kappa 0.52). With outcome knowledge, panels reclassified 18 percent of alerts, almost always towards the known outcome. Disagreement was greatest for small gastrointestinal clusters in older adults. The authors conclude that panel review is a weak reference standard for estimating the accuracy of validation procedures and that outcome-blinded panels still disagree substantially."},{"title":"Checklist-based alert triage in a national surveillance centre: internal evaluation summary","authors":"National Surveillance Centre Signals Team","year":null,"venue":"National Surveillance Centre internal reports","providerType":"report","abstract":"This summary describes the introduction of a checklist for triaging syndromic surveillance alerts in a national surveillance centre. Staff reported that the checklist made handovers easier and that decisions were easier to explain to managers. The summary states that validation became faster and that no outbreaks were missed, but it gives no figures for time, no definition of a missed outbreak and no comparison period. It lists the checklist items, which resemble those of other agencies. The summary carries no date, and the evaluation period and the number of alerts are not reported."},{"title":"Randomising days rather than alerts: contamination and learning effects in trials of surveillance procedures","authors":"Okonkwo-Brennan A, Taniguchi-Voss L","year":2023,"venue":"Tamsford Epidemiologic Methods Letters","doi":"10.5555/eml.2023.0031","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Trials that randomise individual alerts to a new validation procedure risk contamination, because the same staff handle both arms on the same day and carry the new procedure over. Using simulation based on two completed evaluations, we compared individual alert randomisation with randomisation of duty days. Day randomisation reduced contamination because staff used only one procedure on a given day, at the cost of a modest design effect when alerts on the same day are correlated. With about five alerts a day and an intracluster correlation near 0.1, the design effect was about 1.4."},{"title":"Syndromic surveillance signal validation: report of a regional workshop","authors":"Regional Surveillance Network Workshop Group","year":null,"venue":"Regional Surveillance Network workshop reports","providerType":"report","abstract":"This report summarises a one-day workshop of epidemiologists from several regional agencies on validating syndromic surveillance signals. Participants agreed that a shared checklist would be useful and listed checks for duplicates, reporting artefacts, age and place clustering and laboratory confirmation. Participants disagreed on whether signals from small rural emergency departments should be escalated more readily, given small counts. The report records opinions only, gives no data on the performance of any procedure, and carries no date or list of participating agencies."},{"title":"Time to public health action after syndromic alerts for norovirus in long-term care: a case series","authors":"Petrov-Asante D, Wakefield-Obi C","year":2021,"venue":"Brackenmoor Surveillance Practice Journal","doi":"10.5555/jphsp.2021.0088","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed 11 norovirus clusters in long-term care homes that were preceded by a syndromic surveillance alert. In 5 of the 11 clusters, public health action followed the first alert by two days or more, usually because the first alert was dismissed as an artefact. Clusters with action within one day of the first alert had fewer cases on average, although the homes also differed in size and staffing. The authors recommend that gastrointestinal alerts involving older adults in a small area are never dismissed without checking for care homes."}]}
